June 2011 # Macro dictates - The uncertain macro economic outlook offers little incentive for any inventory building through the consumption chain. This is now the sixth consecutive month of increase in total LME inventories. Over the past two days, inflows into LME warehouses have continued, up by 5,725t to 473,500t. LME stocks are now back up to almost exactly the same level they were a year ago. - Demand is slowing in Q2 after a surprisingly upbeat Q1. Supply growth is unspectacular, but with plenty of stocks around, this is not causing any concerns to the market. One could argue – where is the deficit? - China’s net imports of copper cathode totalled 115,600 t in April down 26% on the previous month, with concentrates landings a healthy 465,800t. The onset of the decline in prices occurred as we went to print on the 5th May, with the three month price falling below $9,0

00/t for the first time since the Japanese disaster back in mid-March. Prices subsequently went on to tumble further, as a combination of Chinese inflation and European debt worries began to weigh heavily on demand prospects and sentiment. The fall in copper prices was not in isolation, as investor sentiment turned negative across the LME complex and wider commodity exchanges, triggering a widespread selloff. Prices fell to a low of $8,546/t by 12th May, but the pace of the decline on the LME was not mirrored on the SHFE and the opening of the arbitrage window, albeit briefly, saw the Chinese back in the market. for consumers that has now disappeared as LME prices have once again scaled higher and are now just above $9,000/t. #### Demand struggles to build on Q1 gains… Against a backdrop of high copper prices, demand surprised on the upside through Q1. In the USA, both the brass mill and the wire & cable sectors performed surprisingly well. Demand was very weak a year ago, but year-on-year growth has exceeded expectations. We do understand that some mills are looking for off-grade cathode in the absence of readily available scrap, but this is more a reflection of merchants holding scrap material off the market (in anticipation of higher prices to come), rather than any underlying shortfall in availability. One surprising observation has been the arrival of Russian rod into the USA, particularly given the antidumping duties on this material. The block on Russian rod had supported the unexpected recovery in the US refined consumption, which we estimate increased by 13% year-on-year in Q1. There are concerns that if this rod continues to flow into the USA it will dampen the US recovery for copper. Meanwhile in Russia, there are ongoing arguments regarding potential new tariffs on rod. The government wants to introduce tariffs on rod to raise tax revenues and the copper industry is seen as an easy target. While we have no idea what the duty rate will be and exactly when it might be introduced, we anticipate that this will occur within the next 12 months. The move would make little sense given the scale of Russian rod capacity, but that is unlikely to sway the law makers. Notwithstanding higher rod exports, we understand that Russian domestic demand from the wire and cable sector

has stood up well through Q1, up 40% year-on-year.  We anticipate this trend will continue, with Russian refined demand set to increase by 20% this year.  Russian rod is also being exported into the Middle East (through traders) and depressing local output there, and as a consequence we see demand growth in that region easing in Q2.  Political instability in Egypt has dampened our 2011 cathode demand expectations at rod mills as we understand that the changes in government have led to the suspension and/or renegotiation of utilities contracts.  Saudi Arabia is the only market in the region which is showing any real strength due to government spending on infrastructure and urban development.

As in the US, European demand has been solid, particularly in Germany.  Uptake has started to ease of late amid the economic uncertainty overhanging the southern European economies of Italy, Spain and Greece. Meanwhile, we have heard isolated reports of fabricators turning down business, citing excessive financing costs and poor profit margins at high copper prices.  It appears that the one positive of a $10,000/t copper price has been that semis manufacturers are now requesting improved payment terms.  We have heard that some brass mills have cut terms from 45 to 30 days. 

Surprisingly Japanese semis output has held up much better than our expectations, declining by just 1.4% in Q1 year-o-year.  Even our estimates of a 6% decline for 2011 in refined cathode demand immediately following the disaster may have been somewhat overdone given the available semis indicators to-date. However, consumption will be constrained by power outages planned over the summer months. Meanwhile, the closure of the Onahama smelter has meant that cathode buying activity from the Japanese has been elevated, in order to cover both domestic and external shortfalls on cathode commitments.  The Japanese approached the main Chilean producers directly to deliver against their contracts to Korean and Taiwanese semi manufacturers, rather than go to the merchants/traders who had material readily available. These downstream markets have been hit by the slowdown in semis import demand from China.  Korean semis output has been shrinking sequentially month-on-month, with the latest available data for April showing production declined by almost 10% year-on-year.  Semis output in Taiwan has also suffered, down by 8.2% in the first quarter of this year.  Both of these countries have seen their rod exports to China decline as China ramps up its domestic production.  In addition, there are signs that China is looking to consume more aluminium wirerod, with a significant push for aluminium building wire by some aluminium producers (see **Consumption Trends** for more details). 

The decline in China‟s cathode imports in April have failed to stir up any excitement in the market.  The arb

has remained unfavourable since July last year and, other than during a few days in May when LME prices tumbled and buying opportunities emerged, the Chinese consumer has stayed well out of the cathode market. We have also seen unexceptional demand from the both the wire and cable and brass mills sectors. Indeed in the year to April, China‟s net trade requirement of raw materials (scrap, concentrate, blister & anode) has slumped by around 16% compared to levels a year ago. #### …as spot interest dwindles once again So far in Q2, usually the seasonally stronger period for copper, traders report that there has been only limited spot business at low volumes. Disappointing for the time of year, yet unsurprising as consumers locked in sufficient quantities on contract with producers in anticipation of a very tight year for cathode. A $9,000/t copper price has led to slightly easier scrap flow than many had anticipated and we © 2011 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 16 Copper Monitor June 2011 www.crumonitor.com understand that some consumers, where possible, have been able to consume scrap in place of cathode which they have sold back into the market. It is clear, however, that the ebb and flow of scrap continues to be very closely correlated to movement in copper prices. As copper prices began to slip through May, and scrap was less readily available, cathode traders were rewarded with an uptick in spot business as consumers viewed prices at levels below $9,000/t as a good buying opportunity. As prices recovered, spot interest for cathode has waned. Premiums in northern Europe are trading higher compared to levels last month, up at $80-90/t, reflecting a small decline in exchange inventories and solid demand in Germany. Premiums in Southern Europe are closer to the $50/t level as Italian

, Spanish and Greek requirements are very soft.  In the USA premiums are unchanged at c/lb 5.0-6.5 as the demand outlook has clouded against a backdrop of poor macro-economic indicators. 

Premiums in China for imported material rallied quite abruptly when prices tumbled and the LME/SHFE arb opened for a short period.  Premium levels have remained elevated at around $90-110/t for imported cathode.  Buying has faded, however, as prices have ticked higher over the past couple of weeks.  Any sales that have occurred have been for small quantities and reflect that there is still more material to be drawn down in the country.  We do not anticipate that the Chinese will come back into the market unless there is a significant drop in prices, as consumers are covered. 

#### Prices off again 

Copper prices were back above $9,000/t in the last week of May with prices hitting a four-week high of $9,260/t on 31<sup>st</sup> May.  However, the majority of copper‟s upward momentum came not from any change in the fundamentals, but rather took its cue from macro-economic indicators.  Prices were buoyed by the OECD‟s upbeat growth assessment which stated that the global recovery was "becoming self-sustaining and more broad based”.  Despite the concerns over European debt, the market appears to have taken some comfort from the reports that European Union leaders may decide on an aid package for Greece by the end of this month.  At the same time Greece's debt concerns have not significantly affected the Euro. 

Following a slew of disappointing macro data out of the USA, China, India and Europe, prices are drifting lower and are trading closer to $9,050/t as we go to print.  In China, manufacturing expanded at its slowest pace in nine months in May, with a key purchasing managers' index down to 52, from 52.9 in April.  A separate PMI reading from HSBC and Markit Economics showed manufacturing growth slowing to its weakest level in 10 months.  There were some positive signs from the PMI input sub-index which fell to 60.3 in May vs. 66.2 in April, a signal of moderating inflation at the wholesale level.  Despite this, there are talks of another rate increase in China, possibly as soon as this weekend.  This will undoubtedly weigh on the market and stir up fears that metal may be released into the market if any of the „copper as collateral‟ positions need to be unwound.  Meanwhile, further reports that India‟s manufacturing sector grew at its slowest pace in four months, while May activity in the UK grew at its slowest pace in 20 months, will do little to boost overall sentiment.  Germany's manufacturing sector, while up from levels in April, rose at its slowest rate since October.  The US data has not helped either with the US housing market, a large copper consuming sector, showing no signs of recovery, whilst consumer confidence fell 5.5% month-on-month and 10% below estimates. || ##### **Precious Metals Quarterly: Gold** In 2010, gold recorded its tenth consecutive annual gain, with spot prices up over 400% throughout the past 10 years, substantially outperforming equities, bonds and most other asset classes. This year alone, the price of gold has been setting new all-time records in various currencies on several occasions as concerns regarding economic growth in developed countries made this metal a popular investment option. Europe‟s sovereign debt crisis prompted investors to use gold as a currency hedge. Pressure on the US dollar against various currencies coupled with higher inflation expectations in many countries, including India and China, also keep pushing gold prices higher. But is the present bull run sustainable? And for how long? Data: CRU,WBMS|||||||||||||| © 2011 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 8 of 16 Copper Monitor June 2011 www.crumonitor.com # Consumption trends ## **Copper tube continues steady growth path** World copper tube production has continued to grow steadily in Q1 2011, increasing to 632,000t. This represents growth of 11.4% y-o-y and 3.3% q-o-q. North American production increased by 22.0% y-o-y in Q1, indicating recovering manufacturing activity. The recovery was caused primarily by the positive impact on US production of anti-dumping duties imposed on all copper tube imports from Mexico and China into the US. As a result, US copper tube production grew by 27.4% y-o-y, whereas Mexican production sufferer a decline of 16.5%. Canada‟s output rose by 4.4% y-o-y in Q1, mainly as a consequence of decreased US demand for Mexican and Chinese copper tube. The impact of the antidumping duties was felt especially strongly by Golden Dragon‟s production plant in Mexico, which was built to predominantly supply the US market. However, in March, the company announced plans to relocate production to Thomasville, Alabama, which will allow it to bypass trade barriers with the US. We expect the new plant, which is forecast to produce 45,000t of copper tube annually, to pose a significant threat to domestic producers in the US. European output remains stable at 2.8% growth y-o-y in Q1. Germany, Europe‟s largest copper tube producer, grew 1.9% y-o-y in Q1 due to positive manufacturing activity. However, industry participants have expressed concern about weak demand from the construction sector. Asia continued to outperform the rest of the world in production, accounting for 61.6% of world output in Q1, a slight increase from 60.8% a year earlier. Despite decreased demand from the US, China‟s production experienced 15.2% y-o-y growth in Q1 0211, driven by strong domestic consumption which increased by 19.2% in the same period. However, we expect Chinese consumption to slow in the coming months as a result of the government‟s domestic appliances subsidy programme reaching saturation due to the long replacement cycle associated with white goods, as well as the tightening credit market. China‟s production is nonetheless set for further increases, with the commissioning of Henan Longhui Copper Co. Ltd.‟s 90,000t/y copper and copper alloy tube project set for completion in June 2011. Japan experienced very strong Q1 growth of 13.2% y-o-y, which was supported by strong domestic demand. However, the impact of the 11th March 2011 earthquake was not reflected in Q1 figures, therefore a fall in output is expected in Q2. Nonetheless, we expect Japanese production to pick up in the medium-term due to increased demand from the reconstruction process. South Korea experienced similar levels of output to Japan,

growing 8.9% y-o-y in Q1. 

## **Copper alloy rods, bars and sections up on rising industrial production** 

World output of copper alloy rods, bars and sections (RBS) reached 762,000t in Q1 2011, a 6.4% increase from the previous year.  The rebound in demand comes predominantly from several end-use sectors, especially manufacturing, but remains constrained by a sluggish construction sector. 

Copper alloy RBS production in North America increased by 5.4% y-o-y and 21.4% q-o-q to 63,000t in Q1 2011.  US production, which constitutes 95.2% of North America‟s output, advanced by 5.1% y-o-y in Q1 2011, amounting to 60,000t, up from 57,000t a year earlier.  US copper alloy RBS demand was driven by a 5.4% y-o-y increase in US industrial production in Q1 2011, which fuelled demand from the manufacturing sector.  However, according to Mueller Industries, the recovery of copper alloy RBS

remains constrained by poor demand from the construction sector, with residential construction suffering in the face of high unemployment and the commercial construction sector being hindered by high vacancy rates.  The US construction sector shrank by 8.7% y-o-y in Q1 2011, based on data for the number of dwellings started. 

North East Asian output of copper alloy RBS advanced by 20.4% y-o-y to 133,000t in Q1 2011, representing a continuing recovery from a low of 83,000t in Q1 2009.  Japan recorded a staggering 28.0% y-o-y increase in production, which amounted to 52,000t in Q1 2011.  We expect Japanese output to increase for two main reasons.  Firstly, copper alloy RBS producers have increased production in anticipation of the government‟s plan for a 15% cut in power consumption between July and September 2011.  Major producers, San-Etsu Metal and Ohki Brass and Copper, have already completed billet stockpiling ahead of the rationing.  Secondly, demand remains firm from house renovation since 2010 and has been considerably increased as a consequence of the restoration process in disaster areas affected by the earthquake. 

China‟s output of copper alloy RBS increased by 2.4% y-o-y to 215,000t in Q1 2011, but has fallen by 4.4% from Q4 2010.  The fall was caused primarily by copper hitting record prices in Q1 2011 as well as through tighter credit availability.  China‟s copper alloy RBS sector continues to operate with a trade deficit which amounted to 21,000t in Q1 2011 compared with 19,000t a year earlier. 

Production of copper alloy RBS in Europe has recovered by 4.1% y-o-y and 13.2% q-o-q to 283,000t in Q1 2011.  Production in Italy, Europe‟s top copper alloy RBS producer, advanced by 5.0% y-o-y to 134,000t in Q1 2011, the highest level since Q3 2008. 

## **Aluminium posing increased threat in electrical applications** 

The soaring price of copper has led to growing interest in using aluminium as a substitute in a variety of applications.  The price

ratio between the two metals, which is currently hovering around 4:1, has driven many downstream processors to invest heavily in the research and development of copper substitutes, particularly for use in the transport and construction sectors, which account for around 10% and 30% of copper consumption respectively. Yazaki, Furukawa Electric and Sumitomo Electric have all begun to offer aluminium wiring harnesses to the automotive sector, which are not only more cost-efficient, but also offer a weight reduction in the region of 40%. With regards to the construction sector, Kyowa Electric Wire, a subsidiary of Furukawa Electric, has recently introduced solderable aluminium building wire to the Chinese market, which uses a tin alloy layer plated onto aluminium wire to allow easy soldering. Alcan Cables, a division of Rio Tinto, has also received recommendations for its Stabiloy aluminium alloy cables for use in civil buildings from industry experts at a seminar hosted by the China Electrical Professional Committee of Sichuan Province Civil Engineering and Architectural Society. Copper clad aluminium (CCA) is also becoming increasingly popular in power grid construction, especially in China. Nonetheless, aluminium still faces significant barriers in its effort to substitute copper. Due to aluminium‟s lower conductivity, a greater volume is required to provide equivalent levels of performance, which adds to bulk. # Industry News ## **Consumption** - The **Japanese Electric Wire & Cable Makers Association** reported that copper wire and cable shipments amounted to 55,400t in April 2011, down by 1.4% y-o-y, mainly due to the earthquake. April was the second consecutive month that shipments fell. Declining sales of copper wire and cable were primarily attributed to weakened demand from the domestic electrical machinery and automotive sectors. In addition, according to the **Japan Copper and Brass Association** , copper semis production amounted to 70,699t in April, a rise of 3.1% m-o-m on a seasonally adjusted basis, and almost flat y-o-y. The rebound in copper semis production occurred as companies ramped up output after the government‟s decision to revoke rolling power outages which had been in effect since the Fukushima nuclear power plant was damaged by the tsunami. - According to Antaike, construction of a copper and copper alloy tube project is underway in the Mangzhuang Industrial zone in Xinxiang

city, which is located in Henan province, China. **Henan Longhui Copper Co. Ltd.** , the owner of the project, expects the production capacity of the facility to be 190,000t/y.  The plant will primarily produce large diameter tube and corrosion-resistant alloy tube.  Henan Longhui Copper Co. Ltd. is a wholly owned subsidiary of **Golden Dragon Group** , the Chinese copper semis fabricator who sold 380,000t of copper tube and reported sales revenues of RMB23.5B in 2010.

- US copper imports increased by 30% m-o-m to 66,166t in March 2011.  The figure represented the highest level since March 2009 when it reached 79,975t.  There was a similar trend in brass mill product imports, which rose by 30% m-o-m to 49.3Mlbs in March.  The US trade deficit of brass mill products widened to 19.9Mlbs in March, up by 15.7% on February.  The segment which saw the largest increase in the trade deficit was flat rolled products, which reached 6.5Mlbs, up from 3.8Mlbs in the previous month. 

- German integrated copper producer **Aurubis** reported a 47% y-o-y increase in net income to €258M in H1 FY2010-2011 (1st Oct 2010 - 31st Mar 2011), up from €161M.  H1 revenue increased by 42% y-o-y from €4.5B to €6.5B.  This outcome was mainly the result of higher copper prices and continued demand for copper caused by the global economic recovery.  However, demand from China steadied in Q2 due to a tighter credit environment, as did demand from Europe, due to increasing economic instability.  The wire and cable industry performed well, experiencing strong demand from the automotive and domestic appliance sectors.  Likewise, copper strip was supported by demand from the coinage and special material sectors.  On the other hand, copper tube and flat rolled products struggled to recover as a result of strong competition from lower cost substitutes. 

- Chinese imports of copper and copper products fell by 39.8% y-o-y to 262,676t in April 2011. Moreover, April imports contracted by 13.7% m-o-m.  On the other hand, imports of copper scrap increased by 2.7% y-o-y to 380,000t in April, but fell by 2.6% m-o-m.  January to April imports of copper and copper products amounted to 1.2Mt, which represents a fall of 22.6% y-o-y.  Conversely, January to April imports of copper scrap rose by 1.9% to 1.4Mt from the same period in 2010.

## **Mine Production** 







- Seven contract workers were killed and 13 injured when a bus they were travelling in overturned while returning to Antofagasta city from the **Zaldivar** copper mine.  The Zaldivar mine is operated by Barrick Gold and the contracted workers belonged to **Construccion y Maestranza MDY** , a local contractor.  In 2010, Zaldivar produced 144,244t of EW copper cathode and is expected to produce around 134,000t this year. 

- Protests between 25<sup>th</sup> and 27<sup>th</sup> May 2011 over benefits at **Codelco’s El Teniente mine** in Chile, the largest underground mining operation in the world, have not affected production.  An estimated 2,000-5,000 of the 11,000 contract workers at the plant are involved in the peaceful protest.  The contract workers are demanding a bonus of US$4,700 each in addition to overtime pay that Codelco allegedly does not recognise. Output remains unaffected as it is the 4,000 permanent staff who are directly involved in production.  Nonetheless, company officials are worried that if the protests continue, production may be indirectly affected through a lack of support for operations.  Violent protests by contract workers led to El Teniente‟s temporary shut-down in 2008.  In 2010, El Teniente produced 388,775t of copper-in concentrate and it is expected to produce 401,218t this year.

## **Exploration and Development** 







- **Codelco** has begun early development work on the **Mina Ministro Hales project** worth US$3.2B. Prestripping of 240Mt of waste material began in April and is scheduled for completion in 3 years time.  Most recently, electric power transmission facilities were relocated as part of the early development works.  The company plans to invest US$650M in the project this year.  Mina Ministro Hales will become an open pit mine producing 170,000t of copper-in-concentrate annually over a 14year mine life.  289Mt of ore will be mined during this period, with an average grade of 0.96%. 

- Two power purchase agreements have been approved by the **Energy Regulation Board (ERB)** in Zambia to provide **Zesco** , a state-owned energy supplier, with access to 170MW of energy.  120MW will be sourced from a hydro-electric power plant project in Itezhi-Tezhi, owned by the **Itezhi-Tezhi Power Corporation (ITPC)** , and 50MW will be supplied by the heavy fuel oil powered thermo plant project, owned by the **Ndola Energy Company (NEC)** .  The development of both projects is due to commence later this year.  Zesco is the main electricity supplier to the **Copperbelt Energy Corporation** , which is in turn the leading provider of power to mines in the African Copperbelt.

## **Smelting and Refining** 







- **Xstrata** has announced plans to phase out smelting operations at **Mount Isa** and refining operations in **Townsville** by 2016, in favour of expanding mining and concentrate production in the North Queensland region.  The decision came as a result of overcapacity in the global smelting and refining markets, strong competition from China, as well as rising operating and capital costs.  Xstrata is currently investing AUD589M into the transformation of the **Ernest Henry** mine from an open pit to underground operation, and is considering investing AUD175M on the acquisition of two copper projects from **Exco Resources** .  In 2011, Mount Isa and Townsville are expected to produce around 230,000t of copper blister and 275,000t of refined copper respectively. 

- A new appeal was submitted on 30<sup>th</sup> May calling for the closure of **Codelco’s Ventanas** plant on the grounds of causing pollution to Chile‟s Puchuncavi district for over 30 years.  The appeal is supported by the local community joined by a group of former plant operators.  The Supreme Court of Chile already rejected prior requests for the plant‟s closure and has overruled an earlier court order for the temporary suspension of operations at the plant.  The plant had allegedly released abnormal emissions of SO2 on 23<sup>rd</sup> March whilst re-starting operations after a maintenance closure.  The smelter produces around 105,000-110,000t/y of blister copper, around a third of which are from Codelco‟s Andina mines.  The remainder are supplied by **Enami** and **Anglo American Chile** . 

- According to press reports, **Xiangguang Copper** announced the completion of its refined copper expansion project in at its refinery in Shandong Province, China which lifted annual capacity by 70%, from 350,000t to 600,000t.  The new plant is not operating at full capacity yet, as it is still undergoing trials.  The company produced around 220,000t of refined copper in 2010.
